messages.subject_clean: Natural selection analisys using Geometrics Morphometrics
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!
I have some questions about phenotypic selection analysis, using geometrics morphometrics.

1- First, what possibilities does geomorph offer to carry out these analyzes? The linear models that using RRPP are very useful, but in the case of natural selection, fitness is a response variable, not the shape.

2- The papers that I have read use the PC axes as shape variables. Is there any analysis where I can directly use the coordinates of landmarks?

3- Finally, I have carried out the phenotypic selection analysis using PC axes as shape variables, which is currently the most accessible. If I am interested in predicting the shape from PCs predicted values by selection analysis, is there a way to do it in geomorph? that is, obtain selection coefficients on landmark coordinates?

Thanks!!

messages.body_plain:
Federico,

I’m not sure if I understand completely what you are attempting to do but if you have a measure of fitness and shape variables, you can ask if they are associated with a two-block PLS analysis (two.b.pls in geomorph).  PLS is more like a correlation analysis than a linear model analysis.  You could use PCs of shape as independent variables in a linear model, but I’m not sure what value the coefficients are, as the PCs are not real variables (that independently mean something) but are summary axis of shape variation.  Collectively you might ascertain that the PCs explain significant variation in fitness, but this is no different than saying shape and fitness are correlated, so PLS seems a bit more straightforward, as a result.

The function, shape.predictor, will allow to predict such shapes, whether PLS or fitted values from a linear model are used.

Cheers!
Mike

The problem is to find a citable source that addresses this in highly general terms. Even when the geometric argument is highly general, its generality may not be evident to anyone who does not already grasp the point.  The two papers cited by Dean are criticisms of our work, but rather than seeing those papers as addressing a highly general point, people read them as if they were solely about partial warps and cladistics.  Our mistake was failing to realize that you should not analyze data within a Euclidean space by projecting them onto axes of a coordinate system then analyzing each projection, one at a time. There are probably many ways to say why not to do that, starting with the Pythagorean Theorem, but I haven't found one that makes the point with sufficient generality that it can be cited in any context. I think that we need that argument, paired with one that addresses the opposite problem, multivariate analyses of incommensurate data, which treat that space as if it were Euclidean.  The problem of explaining why not to do either is complicated by the perception that principal components are "real", being (for example, in the case of PC1) the "line of least evolutionary resistance" or "the direction of greatest diversification".

all(mytree$tips == dimnames(myshapedata9)[[3]])

and

all(mytree$tips %in% dimnames(myshapedata9)[[3]])

all(dimnames(myshapedata9)[[3]] %in% mytree$tips)

The first line would verify if names match exactly (in order). The other two would verify if all your shape objects are on the phylogeny and if all tips of the tree are in your shape dataset. If the second is the case, then you would need to filter to make them match.

Gui,

You can only connect a tree to tips in your plot if you have one value per species.  Even though a tree in phylogenetics describes the evolutionary relationships among species, a tree in a statistical sense does not make sense there are N tips for N species.  You have to either come up with a tree that describes the relationship among individuals within species, in addition to species, or collapse your data into species values (perhaps find the means by species).

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am curious about the plotting possibilities for TPS deformation grids. Specifically, I am wondering if it is possible to plot a reference configuration (with links) on top of the target configuration (with links) on TPS deformation grids?

See the attached figure to see what I'm referring to. I believe I generated this example manually but something tells me that there may have been a way to do that in geomorph that I have forgotten as it's been over a year since I last worked on this.

Here is the code I have used to attempt it. I recognize that the points function as you see in the code below, allows me to at least plot the landmarks of the reference configuration over the TPS grids showing the target configurations. Can I weave the links in somehow to join these reference configuration points as seen in the attached figure, so that both the target config in the TPS grids have links as do the overlaid reference configs?

# create plot area
mat <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4), 2)

# set the size of the rows and columns
layout(mat, widths=c(1,1), heights=c(1.5,1.5))
par(mar=c(0,0,0,0))
link.file<-read.csv("links.csv")
links<-matrix(link.file$links, ncol=2, byrow=T)
gp <- gridPar(pt.bg <http://pt.bg> = "blue", pt.size = 1, link.lwd=2, tar.pt.bg <http://tar.pt.bg>="blue", tar.link.lty=2, tar.link.col="blue", link.lty =2, link.col="blue")
ref<-mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords)

#mean shapes
riv.f<-plotRefToTarget(ref,shpmean.riv.f, mag=5, method="TPS", links=links)
points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex=1)
riv.m<-plotRefToTarget(ref,shpmean.riv.m,mag=5, method="TPS", links=links)
points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex=1)
res.f<-plotRefToTarget(ref,shpmean.res.f,mag=5, method="TPS", links=links)
points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex=1)
res.m<-plotRefToTarget(ref,shpmean.res.m,mag=5, method="TPS", links=links)
points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex=1)

Thanks for your thoughts.

Daniel.

The part in Dean’s message that was important was the [,1].  Tables, matrices, data frames, and arrays in R use the brackets and commas to specify locations.  Something like, [5,] means the fifth row and something like [, 8] means the eighth column.  So if you can get to the pc.scores in your plotTangentSpace object, then tacking on [, 1:5] at the end will reduce it to the first 5 components.

More info found here: https://www.statmethods.net/management/subset.html

Mike

I’ll answer the second question first.  No, you cannot have negative distances.  But show.vectors = TRUE in the summary will return the LS means and you can infer which is larger.  You can also look at the model coefficients.

Regarding the error you received I do not know exactly what caused it, but it looks like you are expecting geomorph.data.frame to understand that geo_functions is already a data frame with several columns and it should take those columns and make them separate variables in a new data frame.  Additionally, you are using as.factor in a formula.  I recommend something like the following:

mypca <- gmprcomp(gpa$coords))

mypca$sdev^2 / sum(mypca$sdev^2)

messages.subject: Is there a way to use two points in geomorph to only constrain the orientation of the shape, and not affect shape data?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a way to use two points in geomorph to only constrain the orientation of the shape, and not affect shape data?
messages.body_plain:
I am interesting in looking at variation in morphology of mammalian mandibular symphyses. The mammalian mandibular symphysis has few fixed landmarks that are homogenous across specimens and is mostly ovate. However I've noticed significant variation in the orientation of the symphysis, in some species the longest axis of the symphysis is close to the horizontal, whereas in others it is subvertical or vertical. However, I realized that in geomorph trying to constrain the shape of the symphysis using a Procrustes analyses would result in all of the symphyses being oriented to the same longest axis and therefore the positional information would be lost.

I thought about using an external landmark (the endpoints of the alveolar line of the molars) to define a horizontal with which the position of the symphysis would be constrained by. However, I realized that any intraspecimen variation in this feature (e.g., the length of the molar row) would be picked up as signal in the shape of the symphysis and potentially bias any analyses of shape I perform. I was wondering if there was any way to use landmarks to define a horizontal in the Procrustes analyses in geomorph, but then exclude them from subsequent analyses of shape.

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Is there a way to use two points in geomorph to only constrain the orientation of the shape, and not affect shape data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Russell,

Procedurally, one could use a set of additional landmarks on the mandible (or a horizontal), perform GPA, and then remove the additional non-symphysis landmarks. This will retain the orientation of the symphysis relative to the rest of the mandible in the set of aligned coordinates representing the symphysis (note: I’d use actual landmarks on the mandible not some arbitrary horizontal. That goes back to the days of the Frankfurt plane in anthropology which ended up having about as many challenges as it solved).

However, understand that when doing such things, one is no longer doing a shape analysis, and interpretation of any patterns becomes exceedingly complicated. In essence, the symphysis landmarks extracted from a larger configuration of points have a shape and now a ‘relative’ orientation; which is what your post seemed to wish to retain. However, they also do not have constant size, so there are size differences, and there are positional differences (the full configuration is centered, but that does not guarantee that the symphyses are). So in gaining the ability to retain the orientation one must now also explain which part of the observed variation is due to shape differences, size differences, orientation differences, and positional differences. Thus while procedurally possible, I don’t see this as advancing one’s explanatory power of anatomical variation.

I see two paths forward. One is to use additional landmarks on the rest of the mandible, perform GPA and shape analyses, but focus one’s interpretation on what is happening with respect to the symphysis. Also, adding some analyses of the symphysis relative to the rest of the mandible (e.g., PLS) might be very important in identifying whether any differences in shape/position of the symphysis are correlated with mandibular shape changes.

A second approach would be to use only the symphysis, and translate and scale them only (no standardizing of orientation). This is again technically possible, but only makes sense if the mandibles are in an absolute standard position: something we can never attain (yes, this goes back to problems with the Frankfurt plane and others and why we developed GPA in the first place).

Hope  this helps you ponder your options.

Best,
